title: Conversions, is, as, typeof
hook: Implicit conversions cannot lose information the compiler cares about. Explicit casts can throw. `is`/`as`/`typeof`/`GetType` are how you ask “what is this?” without pretending C# is JS.

sections.heading: Casts and type tests
sections.prose: Numeric promotions (`int` to `long`, `float` to `double`) are implicit. Narrowing (`long` to `int`, `double` to `int`) is explicit and can overflow or truncate — wrap in `checked` if that matters. Reference conversions up the hierarchy are implicit; downcasts are explicit and throw `InvalidCastException` on failure. `is` tests compatibility and, in modern C#, can introduce a variable (`if (msg is string body)`). `as` converts to a reference or nullable type and returns `null` on failure — never use `as` on a non-nullable value type. `typeof(Token)` is the `Type` object for a compile-time name, including `typeof(Dictionary<,>)` for unbound generics. `obj.GetType()` is the run-time type of an instance. `nameof` is a string, not a `Type`. Compile-time type drives overload resolution; run-time type drives virtual dispatch and `is`.

snippets.label: is/as versus GetType versus typeof
snippets.explanation: Wrong: `typeof(payload)` — typeof needs a type name. Wrong: comparing `GetType()` to `typeof(IList)` for interface tests — use `is`.

interviewTakeaways: `typeof` is compile-time; `GetType()` is run-time; `is`/`as` test compatibility.
Failed explicit reference casts throw; `as` yields null.
Narrowing numeric casts truncate; they do not round.
commonPitfalls: Using `GetType() == typeof(Base)` and missing derived types — want `is`.
`as` on `int` — does not compile; use a nullable or a cast.
Parsing CSV with `(int)double.Parse` and losing fractional grades — use `decimal`.

jsTsCorrelations.note: `typeof` in JS is a string tag. C# `typeof` returns `System.Type`. `instanceof` is closer to `is` for references.
